# PRD: Coherent Canvas Zoom And Text Visibility

## Problem Statement

When a designer zooms out, Annotations and Pinned Plant Names retain their screen size and remain visible, crowding the canvas. The zoom percentage depends on the initial window dimensions, so the same percentage does not consistently represent the same magnification. Wheel input applies one fixed zoom step per event and treats ordinary trackpad scrolling as zoom.

Text visibility must also be evaluated alongside Plant Symbols, Annotation markers, Zone boundaries, selection cues, handles, and measurement aids so the canvas remains visually coherent from a site overview to precision editing.

## Solution

Provide consistent, smooth canvas navigation and progressively simplify text presentation at overview scales. Annotations and Pinned Plant Names keep their readable text size, then fade out across one shared range of absolute canvas scales. Hidden Annotations retain subtle selectable markers. A single directly selected object's text, or an Annotation being edited, remains readable; selecting multiple objects does not reveal all their text.

Keep the zoom percentage with a fixed reference for 100%, alongside the distance scale bar. Ordinary scrolling pans. Ctrl/Cmd + wheel and trackpad pinch zoom in proportion to the gesture, preserving the canvas point under the pointer.

Begin delivery with an agent-led visual tuning pass across representative Designs. Compare text, symbols, markers, outlines, badges, handles, and measurements together, and retain or adjust presentation sizing only where the evidence supports the change. Physical geometry and distances continue to scale accurately with the camera. This pass produces recommended defaults and reproducible visual evidence before production values are finalized.

## User Stories

1. As a designer, I want Annotations and Pinned Plant Names to disappear smoothly when I zoom out, so that I can see the overall planting and spatial arrangement.
2. As a designer, I want hidden Annotations to leave subtle selectable markers, so that I can find and read notes without first zooming in.
3. As a designer, I want the text of one directly selected object, or an Annotation I am editing, to remain readable, so that zoom does not interrupt identification or editing.
4. As a designer, I want multiple selection to preserve the overview's reduced text density, so that selecting an arrangement does not cover it with names and notes.
5. As a designer, I want an equal zoom percentage to mean equal magnification across windows and Designs, so that the zoom indicator is predictable while the scale bar explains physical distance.
6. As a mouse or trackpad user, I want scrolling to pan and modified scrolling or pinching to zoom smoothly around my pointer, so that I can navigate without abrupt jumps or losing my point of interest.
7. As a designer, I want Plant Symbols, Annotation markers, outlines, badges, and editing handles to remain distinguishable across zoom levels, so that overview clarity and precise editing work together.
8. As a designer, I want visual simplification to preserve Design content, physical measurements, Layer visibility, and editing constraints, so that zooming changes presentation without changing my Design.

## Success Criteria

- A reproducible visual comparison covers a sparse garden, a dense planting, and a large site at overview, working, and precision scales. It records the selected zoom reference, fade range, navigation sensitivity, and the retained or adjusted presentation sizes with reasons and screenshots.
- Unselected Annotations and Pinned Plant Names fade through the same scale interval, reach fully hidden text at the overview threshold, and return on zoom-in without shrinking to unreadable text or flickering near the threshold.
- Hidden Annotation markers remain discoverable and selectable wherever existing visibility and editing policy permits. A single direct selection reveals the appropriate text without duplicate plant names; editing keeps Annotation text readable. Multiple and Object Group selection follow normal fading.
- Repeated navigation, fading, and selection do not change saved content, pinning choices, dirty state, or undo history. Hidden Layers and locked-object rules remain effective.
- Equal percentages produce equal canvas magnification independent of initial window size. The scale bar and measurements remain consistent with actual geometry, and existing precision zoom limits remain available.
- Ordinary scrolling pans; Ctrl/Cmd + wheel and pinch zoom proportionally around a stable pointer anchor. Zero movement produces no camera change, zoom limits remain effective, and small gestures do not become full fixed zoom steps.
- The visual comparison demonstrates readable selection and editing cues without disproportionate symbol, marker, badge, or handle growth. Physical Zone and Measurement Guide geometry stays correctly scaled, and existing measurement visibility rules remain intact.
- Pixi and Canvas2D agree on visible presentation and interaction geometry, including after viewport-only updates, resizing, and renderer fallback. Map alignment and Fit to content remain correct after the presentation changes.

## Implementation Decisions

- CameraController remains the authority for viewport transforms, scale limits, and transient viewport publication. Zoom controls project its scale consistently; the in-canvas map follows that camera through the existing map adapter.
- SceneInteractionSession continues to own navigation input and listener lifetime. Gesture normalization and camera updates must preserve existing interaction cancellation and teardown behavior.
- Renderer-independent scene presentation and geometry are the seams for zoom-dependent visibility, Visual Footprint, and Annotation layout. Pixi and Canvas2D consume consistent results rather than choosing independent thresholds or sizing rules.
- Rendering and interaction must agree on whether an Annotation presents text or a marker. Hit testing, selection outlines, group bounds, arrangement placement, and camera framing must use a coherent interpretation of that presentation.
- Plant Symbols remain symbolic position markers with a smooth absolute-scale Visual Footprint and a low-scale dot fallback. The current radius curve is the comparison baseline, not a preselected defect. Any recommended change must propagate through the existing shared footprint rather than alter glyph drawing alone.
- Physical Design geometry follows the camera scale; text, strokes, badges, handles, and other readability aids retain appropriate screen-space visual weight. Global coherence does not require every category to use an identical scaling curve.
- Selection-based text revelation applies only to one directly selected Placed Plant or Annotation, plus active Annotation editing. Pinned plants reveal their Pinned Plant Name; unpinned plants retain their existing Selection Label. No general automatic plant-name labeling is introduced.
- The change is presentation and navigation work. Existing persistence authorities, Design data, Layer visibility, Design Object Locks, native execution rules, and built-in symbol contracts remain in force. No runtime dependency or file-format change is currently justified.

## Testing Decisions

- Test observable behavior through the camera, scene presentation/query, and interaction seams used by production callers; avoid tests that merely mirror private constants or formulas.
- Build on existing camera, zoom-control, Selection Label, Annotation geometry, renderer, measurement, and map-camera coverage. Exercise scale boundaries, repeated zoom reversal, single versus mixed/multiple/group selection, pinning, editing, hidden Layers, and locked objects.
- Verify pointer anchoring, two-axis pan, modifier handling, gesture magnitude and delta units, zero movement, limits, and lifecycle cleanup through navigation behavior. Include evidence that native/browser zoom does not consume intended canvas gestures on supported hosts.
- Check that visible Annotation text or markers match hit targets and selection bounds, with rotated and multiline Annotations and Fit to content from different starting scales. Verify zoom and presentation changes do not dirty the Design or add history entries.
- Visually compare long names and notes, small and large windows, light and dark themes, and normal, fractional, and high pixel densities. Exercise both rendering backends and viewport-only refreshes. Measure navigation responsiveness on the same dense scene before and after changes rather than inventing an unsupported performance target.
- Production frontend changes require TypeScript checking, focused regression coverage, and the full frontend suite because this touches shared canvas runtime behavior. Throwaway tuning code is evidence, not production implementation, and follows the repository's prototype discipline.
- Agent-led browser inspection can select visual defaults and verify event behavior. Record the limits of simulated gestures; a short physical mouse/trackpad check is useful evidence for feel, not a reason to ask the user to choose numerical parameters.

## Out of Scope

- Changing physical Zone dimensions, plant placement, Measurement Guide distances, persisted Annotation text/font choices, or saved pinning choices as a result of zoom.
- Reintroducing canopy-spread display modes, general plant labeling, uploaded symbols, or a new renderer.
- Collision-based label placement, user-facing tuning settings, map rotation, unrelated app chrome redesign, or rewriting all canvas presentation modules.
- Applying text fading to Measurement Guides, Zone Measurements, rulers, or the scale bar; their existing visibility semantics remain the baseline during the coherence review.
- Expanding the precision zoom limits, changing basemap sources/projection, or redesigning Design export.

## Further Notes

- The PRD carries forward the accepted decisions recorded by canopi-6qx3 and adds a bounded review of visual coherence across canvas presentation categories. The previous precision-zoom work in canopi-ag6z established the current maximum; its earlier exclusions for gestures and default zoom were slice-specific, not a prohibition on this work.
- Numerical values remain open: the absolute scale for 100%, the shared fade endpoints and interpolation, Annotation marker size, navigation sensitivity, and any evidence-supported adjustments to symbol/outline/badge/handle presentation. Do not represent illustrative candidates as already validated defaults.
- Initial tuning should be agent-led and produce a reusable scene corpus, comparisons, and a recommendation. Evaluate existing values alongside alternatives; preserving a value is a valid outcome. Record which results are visually verified and which still need physical-device feedback.
- Resolve the Annotation marker-to-text interaction transition, framing of hidden text, and behavior at dense marker overlap during tuning. Avoid invisible text intercepting clicks intended for visible objects. Existing Layer and lock policy remains authoritative throughout.
- Distinguish trackpad pinch events from browser page zoom and evaluate supported desktop WebViews and Web Edition. Canvas map synchronization must remain exact; smoothing must not introduce independent camera drift or suppress small camera updates.
- Suggested delivery order for subsequent to-issues slicing: visual/input calibration first; consistent camera readout and navigation; complete text fading and marker interaction across both renderers; evidence-supported visual coherence adjustments; integrated acceptance verification. These are capabilities to slice, not implementation beads created by this PRD. Numerical calibration must precede final acceptance of dependent presentation defaults.
- Update the pending canvas guidance and any numeric sizing guidance when implementation lands. This PRD and its unresolved tuning values do not claim that the feature is implemented.
acceptance_criteria: Reproducible visual and input calibration records justified defaults. Annotation and Pinned Plant Name fading, marker discovery, single-selection/editing exceptions, and multi-selection behavior match the PRD. Zoom percentage is window-independent; scroll pans and modified wheel/pinch zoom proportionally around the pointer. Physical geometry, measurements, precision limits, map alignment, persistence, locks, and Layer policy remain correct. Both renderer backends and interaction geometry agree; required frontend gates pass. Complete the global visual-coherence review and apply only evidence-supported sizing changes.

title: Fix: Keep Canvas2D screen-space presentation aligned on HiDPI displays
description:
## Problem

When the Canvas2D scene renderer is active on a display whose device pixel ratio is greater than one, a Pinned Plant Name does not remain visually attached below its Placed Plant. Zooming or panning makes the displacement increasingly obvious. The persisted pin state and the label's logical viewport coordinate remain correct; the visible label is drawn at the wrong screen position.

Pinned Plant Names should retain the same CSS-pixel relationship to their Placed Plants at standard, fractional, and high device pixel ratios, before and after viewport changes. Existing screen-space canvas presentation should follow the same invariant.

## Steps to Reproduce

A deterministic renderer-level harness exercised the public Canvas2D renderer interface with one pinned Placed Plant, a device pixel ratio of 2, and a zoomed and panned viewport. The Placed Plant center appeared at CSS x = 70 while its Pinned Plant Name appeared at x = 35. The failure reproduced on all three attempts.

Controls established the scope:

- The same zoom and pan sequence remained aligned at device pixel ratio 1.
- Device pixel ratio 2 failed even without a viewport change, showing that zoom and pan expose rather than create the error.
- Preserving the device-pixel transform for the label made the failing scenario pass.
- The Pixi renderer kept the Pinned Plant Name aligned through the same viewport sequence.

## Root Cause Analysis

The Canvas2D renderer scales its backing store and initial drawing transform by the display device pixel ratio. World presentation retains that scale. Screen-space presentation then replaces the transform with an identity transform while continuing to supply coordinates expressed in CSS pixels. On a high-density backing store, those CSS coordinates are therefore interpreted as physical backing-store pixels and are divided by the device pixel ratio when displayed.

At device pixel ratio 2, the visible Pinned Plant Name position is exactly half the intended screen coordinate. The camera and label projection are current, ruling out stale viewport state, accumulated floating-point error, and font metrics as causes.

The same screen-space transform pattern is shared by existing Selection Labels, Annotation text, Measurement Guide labels, and Placed Plant stack badges, so the durable correction belongs to the Canvas2D screen-space projection contract rather than a Pinned Plant Name special case.

## Agent Brief

**Summary:** Keep Canvas2D screen-space presentation aligned with scene objects on HiDPI displays.

**Desired behavior:**
Canvas2D should expose one coherent screen-space projection contract: callers continue to express presentation in CSS pixels, while the renderer consistently maps those coordinates into its density-scaled backing store. Pinned Plant Names and existing screen-space presentation must stay visually anchored through zoom, zoom out, and pan at standard, fractional, and high device pixel ratios. - The Canvas2D scene renderer instance used for full scene renders and viewport-only updates

- Pinned Plant Name and Visual Footprint presentation contracts

## TDD Fix Plan

1. **RED**: Through the Canvas2D renderer instance, render one pinned Placed Plant at device pixel ratio 2, apply a zoomed and panned viewport, and assert that the visible label center remains horizontally aligned with the marker and below its Visual Footprint.
   **GREEN**: Preserve the backing-store density scale when drawing Pinned Plant Names in screen space.

2. **RED**: At a fractional Windows-style device pixel ratio, assert that the same Pinned Plant Name alignment contract holds after a viewport update.
   **GREEN**: Generalize the density-preserving screen-space projection without rounding away fractional ratios.

3. **RED**: Exercise existing Selection Label and Annotation presentation at high device pixel ratio and assert their observable CSS-pixel anchors remain stable.

4. **RED**: Exercise Measurement Guide labels and Placed Plant stack badges at high device pixel ratio and assert their observable anchors and pixel-sized presentation remain stable.
   **GREEN**: Route the remaining screen-space presentation paths through the shared contract.

**REFACTOR**: Keep the density conversion private to the Canvas2D renderer, remove duplicated transform resets, and retain the renderer instance as the behavior-bearing test seam.

**Out of scope:**
- Changing renderer backend selection or fallback policy
- Changing Pinned Plant Name persistence, localization, or layout rules
- Redesigning label collision behavior or Visual Footprint sizing

title: Decide Canvas Runtime app adapter composition
description:
## Decision

Canopi will compose both Desktop and Web Canvas Runtime app adapters through one app-owned, platform-neutral factory. The factory returns the existing Canvas Runtime App Adapter contract and owns clean-state publication, Design composition, translation, settings reads and writes, reactive settings subscriptions, and Layer projection. Each edition supplies only its actual Species-presentation and Saved Object Stamp capabilities at its compile-time composition root. The Web adapter must omit an unavailable Saved Object Stamp capture capability instead of advertising a no-op operation. Both editions will wrap the concrete Scene Canvas Runtime through one runtime-owned host adapter.

## Rationale

Desktop and Web currently duplicate the same app-owned settings, subscription, Layer, clean-state, Design-composition, and translation implementation. Only Species presentation and Saved Object Stamp support differ. Two production compositions justify one in-process seam, improve locality for Canvas Runtime app policy, and prevent edition drift without merging the edition hosts or importing platform code into runtime core.

## Alternatives Considered

- Keep the two complete adapters: rejected because every shared settings or Layer-policy change must be made and tested twice.
- Share only a settings sub-object: rejected because clean state, Design composition, translation, and Layer projection would still be duplicated and the interface would expose the factory's internal split.
- Select Desktop or Web with runtime environment checks: rejected because ADR 0021 requires compile-time platform adapters and Web builds must remain statically free of Tauri and IPC dependencies.
- Make Saved Object Stamp capture a required no-op capability in Web: rejected because it exposes an action that cannot perform its advertised behavior.
design:
## Interface Contract

An app-owned factory accepts a small capability object containing optional Saved Object Stamp capture and edition-appropriate Species presentation sources, and returns the existing Canvas Runtime App Adapter. It owns the shared app policy for clean-state publication, canonical Design composition, translation, settings reads and commands, exact reactive subscriptions, and app-owned Layer projection. Capability objects are fixed for an adapter lifetime. The factory performs no platform detection and imports no Web, Tauri, IPC, or native Species adapters.

Desktop composition supplies IPC-backed Plant labels and Species cache plus the live Saved Object Stamp Workbench. Web composition supplies browser-safe or detached Species presentation and omits Saved Object Stamp capture until a real browser workbench is mounted. Absence is observable through the existing optional runtime capability so contextual actions stay hidden instead of dispatching a no-op.

A runtime-owned host adapter wraps a concrete Scene Canvas Runtime and its projected surfaces. Desktop and Web creation roots both use that wrapper while continuing to own their distinct construction inputs and lifetimes.

## Hidden Complexity

The shared factory hides settings-signal reads, Settings Projection mutations, theme/locale/chrome effect setup, Layer projection ownership, clean-state publication, Design save composition, and translation wiring. Edition roots expose only the capabilities that truly differ.

## Dependency Strategy

This is an in-process seam with two production compositions. Desktop capabilities are native/IPC-backed; Web capabilities are browser-safe. Focused tests supply in-memory capability probes. Runtime core continues to depend only on its Canvas Runtime App Adapter contract, and compile-time platform entries remain separate under ADR 0021.

## Consequences And Migration

Migrate Desktop first through characterization of its capabilities, then make Web consume the same factory and delete its duplicate settings, subscription, and Layer code. Move the identical concrete-runtime host wrapper behind a runtime-owned factory. Do not merge App Shells, Design Session lifecycles, Canvas command composition, or Species Catalog storage adapters. Do not add runtime dependencies.

Update Canvas Runtime and Design Session agent guidance in the same change. Architecture policies must keep the shared factory platform-neutral, require both edition compositions to consume it, forbid Web from rebuilding app settings policy, and keep the Web production graph free of Desktop IPC.

## Testing Strategy

Write factory-interface tests first for capability identity, settings commands, subscriptions, Layer synchronization, clean state, and Design composition. Characterize Desktop Species/Saved Stamp capabilities and Web detached Species/absent Saved Stamp behavior. Migrate existing Browser Canvas settings coverage to the shared interface and delete tests that only restate the removed duplicate implementation. Retain focused edition tests for actual capability differences. Run focused/full frontend tests, TypeScript, declarative architecture policies, Web boundary build, and Desktop production build.

description:

title: Include complete scene geometry in projection extent diagnostics
description:
## Slice Summary

## Steps to Reproduce

## User Value

## Out of Scope

design:
## Behavioral Contract

Deepen zone-geometry with a narrow effective boundary/extent operation for polygon, line, rotated rectangle, and rotated ellipse shapes. Projection precision accepts extent meters and owns only scalar policy; MapLibre Canvas Surface composes the two.

Preserve radial-from-origin semantics, the stable projection id, and the strict warning threshold. Keep projection.ts runtime-dependency free and add an architecture policy proving Scene extent consumes canonical Zone geometry.

## TDD Order
Characterize empty, Plant, polygon Zone, and Annotation-anchor extents. Add red Measurement Guide endpoint, rotated rectangle, and true rotated ellipse extrema cases. Extract Scene extent, convert projection precision to scalar input, then migrate MapLibre composition and policies.

title: Decision: Enforce architecture from parsed source facts
description:
## Decision
Replace regex/manual-list architecture checks with a small declarative policy harness over parsed TypeScript imports and automatically discovered CSS declarations, retaining focused behavior tests and only meaningful tombstones.

## Rationale
Current source-text tests are simultaneously brittle and incomplete: formatting or movement breaks them while new files, re-exports, and many CSS modules escape coverage.

## Alternatives Considered
- Keep adding source-string assertions: grows a tombstone inventory.
- Remove architecture tests: weakens proven dependency guardrails.
- Add a broad new lint stack: unnecessary if existing TypeScript tooling can expose the required facts.
design:
## Selected Design

Build focused test utilities, not a general linter. Use the installed TypeScript compiler API to extract static imports, type imports, dynamic imports, and re-exports into normalized module edges. Express dependency directions and confined importers as named data policies. Discover all active source files automatically.

For CSS, discover every `*.module.css` and parse declarations with a small tested scanner or an already direct project dependency; do not rely on a transitive package or add a dependency without justification. Policy data may declare narrow semantic exceptions for structural one-pixel values.

Retain behavior tests and only tombstones where absence itself is a durable contract. Delete exact symbol placement/text assertions that duplicate behavior.

## Invariants

- Each migrated rule is equivalent or stronger.
- New files are covered without editing an allowlist.
- Parser fixtures cover multiline, comments, aliases, type-only, dynamic, and re-export syntax.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Parsed source facts, declarative policies, discovery, and exception policy are recorded.
- [ ] No-weakening migration invariant is explicit.
- [ ] General-linter and guard-removal alternatives are rejected.
- [ ] The implementation bead depends on this decision and final architecture slices.

title: Make frontend architecture policies declarative and complete
description:
## Slice Summary
Introduce tested source-fact parsers and compact boundary/CSS policies, migrate existing enforceable rules one-for-one, discover new files automatically, and delete obsolete text-placement assertions without weakening behavior coverage.

## User Value
Architecture failures become precise and new modules are guarded automatically, while sound refactors stop requiring edits to implementation-shaped snapshots.

## Out of Scope
A general-purpose linter, dependency additions without justification, or weakening any existing boundary/visual-token rule.
design:
## Behavioral Contract

Introduce test-only architecture utilities with self-tests. Parse TypeScript/TSX imports via the compiler API and resolve repository-relative modules consistently. Migrate true dependency-direction/import-confinement rules from `frontend-boundaries-sources.test.ts` into named policy tables. Move behavior checks to focused tests where missing; retain deliberate source tombstones separately.

Discover all CSS modules recursively and parse full declarations across lines/comments. Preserve the intent of font/spacing/radius/transition tokens with explicit, reviewed exceptions for structural values. Remove the Wave 4 milestone/manual list vocabulary.

## TDD Order

Prove parser fixtures first, then migrate one policy at a time while keeping the old assertion until equivalence passes. Do the same for CSS discovery/parser, then delete superseded source assertions.
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] Static, type-only, literal/non-literal dynamic imports and named/default/namespace/star re-exports are parsed from the TypeScript AST with self-tests.
- [x] Dependency, importer, ownership, write, call, export, and tombstone policies are compact data with precise locations and resolved targets.
- [x] All active TypeScript-family and CSS Module files are discovered automatically.
- [x] Multiline/commented CSS declarations are parsed; exact at-rule-aware structural and behavior exceptions are explicit and single-use.
- [x] Every removed source-string assertion has equivalent or stronger policy or focused behavior coverage.
- [x] No architecture, type, build, or visual-token guardrail is weakened.
- [x] Obsolete Wave/milestone and exact-placement assertions are removed.
- [x] Harness tests, full frontend tests, TypeScript, Desktop build, Web build, and artifact boundary scan pass.
- [x] Frontend and Canvas Runtime agent guidance documents the resulting policy seams.
notes: Replaced the 1,367-line regex/manual-list boundary test and 59-line Wave 4 milestone test with compiler-AST source facts, recursive source/CSS discovery, declarative policies, focused Web entry/build tests, and fail-closed CSS token rules. Export identity follows named, default, namespace, wildcard, imported aliases, transparent defaults, and transparent exported variable aliases. CSS rules validate canonical unconditional root tokens, case-sensitive custom properties, at-rule-specific one-use exceptions, numeric dimensions/times, and math-function scale arithmetic. Token substitutions preserve rendered values. Final validation: 194 frontend test files and 1,815 tests passed; npx tsc --noEmit; npm run build; npm run build:web including the artifact scanner; git diff --check. Three independent final review passes ended CLEAN. Updated docs/agent/frontend-patterns.md and docs/agent/canvas-runtime.md.

title: Own the complete ruler drag lifecycle
description:

## Out of Scope

design:
## Behavioral Contract

Create a deep ruler overlay owner in `rulers.ts`; retain pure scale/tick helpers as pure functions. Track drag listeners and cursor restoration explicitly. Integrate SceneChrome with direct viewport snapshots and remove its three-closure StageView adapter and mutable raw callback wiring.

Test through the public overlay interface in jsdom. Keep renderer-independent visual output and scale-bar behavior unchanged; reduce module-wide mocks only where focused behavior now replaces them.

## TDD Order

Start with down→destroy listener cleanup, then repeated-down cancellation, mouseup, blur, guide conversion after viewport update, visibility, DPR resizing, and idempotent destroy.

- [x] Destroy during an active drag removes document/window listeners and restores cursor state.
- [x] Repeated drag starts retain at most one active drag.
- [x] Mouseup/blur cancellation and guide publication semantics are covered.
- [x] Ruler updates consume canonical viewport state; StageView and per-render adapter closures are removed.
- [x] Raw DOM lifecycle parts are hidden behind one idempotent owner.
- [x] Existing ruler/grid/scale visuals and guide coordinates remain unchanged.
- [x] Focused ruler/SceneChrome tests, full frontend tests, TypeScript, and Web build pass.

notes: Implemented the deep RulerOverlay owner test-first, including failure-atomic construction, exact cursor restoration, restart/mouseup/blur/hide/destroy cancellation, canonical camera snapshots, normalized zero-size rendering, and SceneChrome/coordinator ownership tests. Three independent review passes ended CLEAN.
close_reason: Shipped one failure-atomic RulerOverlay lifecycle owner using canonical camera snapshots; covered teardown, restart, blur, hide, replacement, DPR/grid geometry, collapsed viewports, guide conversion, and constructor rollback. Full frontend tests, focused tests, TypeScript, Desktop/Web builds, boundary check, and three CLEAN reviews passed.

title: Use one Settings Projection in Desktop and Web
description:

## User Value
Preferences normalize and persist consistently in both editions, including browser canvas settings that currently vanish.

## Out of Scope

design:
## Behavioral Contract

Define a small settings platform port (load/save, with lifecycle only if needed) and compile-time Desktop/browser adapter modules. Remove direct IPC from Settings Projection. Desktop bootstrap continues health/shortcut ownership while delegating settings load; browser bootstrap hydrates a complete normalized Settings value from browser storage/defaults and installs theme synchronization.

Migrate BrowserAppShell locale/theme commands and browser canvas snap/Plant Spacing commands through `mutateSettingsProjection`. Remove `WebApp` settings callbacks and duplicated locale/theme validators. Keep browser app-data as the storage mechanism; do not redesign it.

## TDD Order

Add adapter conformance tests, browser default/hydration test, locale/theme persistence, snap/Plant Spacing persistence, Desktop adapter delegation, and flush/no-op behavior one at a time.
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] Settings Projection has no direct Tauri IPC or browser-storage dependency.
- [x] Typed Desktop and browser adapters satisfy one contract and are exercised by checks/tests.
- [x] Desktop and Web bootstrap through the same hydration policy.
- [x] Web locale, theme, snap, and Plant Spacing mutations normalize and persist through Settings Projection.
- [x] Duplicated Web validators/callback persistence and direct settings signal writes are removed.

- [x] Focused settings/platform/Web shell/canvas tests, full frontend tests, both TypeScript/build variants pass.

notes: Implemented typed Desktop/browser Settings adapters and one shared projection lifecycle. Added generated Rust defaults/enums, generated-backed frontend signal defaults, synchronous Web hydration, first-paint theme cache, serialized/coalesced retryable persistence, replacement-safe handoff, retirement-aware flush, and owned/coalesced Desktop close handling. TDD/review regressions cover bootstrap mutations/no-ops/load failures, write failures/reentry/replacement races, queued mutations during flush, HMR/listener lifetimes, close failures, Web locale/theme/snap/Plant Spacing, adapters, defaults, and first paint. Updated docs/agent/document-lifecycle.md and docs/agent/frontend-patterns.md.

title: Delete the hypothetical ProjectionBackend facade
description:
## Slice Summary
Migrate camera, Target-map, precision, and diagnostics callers to narrow canonical projection operations, then remove the one-adapter backend interface/object/selector and identity tests.

## User Value

## Out of Scope
Changing local-Mercator math, adding a new projection, changing precision thresholds, or altering map/canvas sync.
design:
## Behavioral Contract

Migrate MapLibre camera, Target map projection, surface diagnostics, and tests away from backend selection. Preserve a stable diagnostic id constant if developer tooling consumes it.

Replace backend-identity tests with behavioral/diagnostic coverage and a focused source/import guard only if it protects the architectural absence rather than implementation placement. Update MapLibre guidance from “backend choice” to “projection math/diagnostics centralized.”

## TDD Order

First update/add behavior tests for diagnostics and callers, observe failure when selection exports are removed, then migrate one caller at a time and delete the facade.

Existing pure implementations are now the canonical exports; production callers import only required operations/constants; diagnostics use stable LOCAL_MERCATOR_PROJECTION_ID and projectionId terminology. Green: 58 focused tests, TypeScript, full frontend 191 files / 1,839 tests, Desktop build, Web build/boundary check, and git diff check passed. Three independent final reviews ended CLEAN. title: Decision: Expose canonical projection operations directly
description:
## Decision
Keep projection.ts as the single local-Mercator seam but remove ProjectionBackend, the sole forwarding adapter, and active-backend selection; expose narrow pure operations and diagnostics directly.

## Rationale
A wide one-adapter interface and a second wrapper surface add synchronized edit points without a selectable backend or external dependency boundary.

## Alternatives Considered
- Keep the facade for hypothetical future projections: pays complexity before a second adapter exists.
- Inject projection strategies into every caller: spreads choice mechanics further.
- Inline math into consumers: destroys the useful canonical projection seam.
design:
## Selected Design

Retain `canvas/projection.ts` as a pure canonical module. Export the current local-Mercator operations, precision product, backend diagnostic id constant, and warning threshold directly. Delete `ProjectionBackend`, `LOCAL_MERCATOR_PROJECTION_BACKEND`, and `getActiveProjectionBackend`.

Callers depend only on the operations they need. Diagnostics report the canonical projection id without implying runtime selection. A future second projection must arrive with a demonstrated selection boundary and can introduce a strategy then.

## Invariants

- Bearing-aware local-Mercator math and precision threshold are behaviorally identical.
- No caller owns duplicate projection math.
- Tests assert round trips, screen lock, zoom, and diagnostics—not adapter identity.

title: Decision: Give ruler overlays one lifecycle owner
description:
## Decision
Replace the raw StageView-shaped ruler surface with one overlay owner that consumes canonical viewport snapshots and owns DOM creation, update, guide-drag cancellation, and teardown.

## Rationale
Destroying rulers during an active drag leaves document listeners and cursor state behind; current ownership is split between SceneChrome and exposed ruler parts.

## Alternatives Considered
- Patch only destroy: retains split mutable ownership and repeated-drag hazards.
- Add a generic DOM-overlay manager: broader than the demonstrated ruler lifecycle.
- Keep StageView terminology: preserves renderer-era adapter closures.
design:
## Selected Design

Replace the shallow `HtmlRulers`/`StageView` surface with one `RulerOverlay` owner. Construction owns canvases/listeners, `update(snapshot)` accepts canonical `SceneViewportState` and screen dimensions/visibility, `refreshTheme()` refreshes cached colors, `setGuideCreate()` sets the app callback, and `destroy()` is terminal/idempotent.

The owner tracks at most one active drag and a single cancellation function. A new pointer/mouse down cancels the previous drag; mouseup, blur, and destroy remove every document/window listener and restore cursor state before publishing a guide.

## Invariants

- No active drag listener outlives the owner.
- Destroy during drag never publishes a guide.
- Guide conversion uses the latest canonical viewport snapshot.
- DOM nodes and callbacks are not exposed as mutable lifecycle parts.

title: Consolidate canvas viewport publication
description:
## Slice Summary
Publish viewport state and revision atomically from the canonical camera owner, migrate query/UI/render consumers, and remove SceneSession/global/revision mirrors and dead viewport inputs.

## User Value
Pan, zoom, resize, and reference-scale behavior have one authority and one observable revision, reducing desynchronization risk and fixture burden.

## Out of Scope
Changing camera behavior, persistence format, gesture semantics, or renderer selection.
design:
## Behavioral Contract

Refactor CameraController around a caller-shaped snapshot containing viewport, screen size/reference scale as required, and revision. Scene runtime publishes or delegates this snapshot without mirroring it into SceneSession state. Query Surface returns the same canonical revision field.

Migrate ZoomControls to a runtime/query-derived read model and command seam rather than `canvas/view-state.ts`. Remove obsolete test fixtures/assertions only after equivalent behavior is covered at CameraController, SceneRuntime, Query Surface, and component boundaries. Rename `stageScale` to `viewportScale` only where this change touches active interfaces.

## TDD Order

Prove initial snapshot, then pan, zoom, resize, reference update, and no-op behavior one mutation at a time. Add a ZoomControls query-fake test before deleting global signals.

- [ ] Camera/viewport code is the only authority for viewport state and its revision.
- [ ] State and revision publish atomically and increment exactly once per effective mutation.

- [ ] ZoomControls consumes the documented Canvas Runtime/Query seam.

Verified 1,768 frontend tests, TypeScript via build:web, Web boundary build, focused TDD regressions, and three independent CLEAN reviews.

title: Decision: Share Settings Projection across platform adapters
description:
## Decision
Extend the accepted Settings Projection so policy is platform-neutral and typed Desktop/Web persistence adapters are selected at compile time; both entries hydrate, mutate, and flush through the same seam.

## Rationale
Desktop policy imports IPC while Web duplicates locale/theme parsing and persistence and directly writes other settings signals. This is a distinct platform extension of canopi-104.

## Alternatives Considered
- Retain separate Web settings code: continues normalization and persistence drift.
- Import Desktop IPC from the shared module: cannot serve the Web build.
- Abstract all platform services at once: expands scope beyond settings.
design:
## Selected Design

Extend the accepted Settings Projection (`canopi-104`) with a narrow typed persistence/bootstrap port selected by the existing compile-time platform pattern. Projection policy owns normalization, signal application, snapshotting, queued writes, and flush. Desktop and browser adapters own only load/save and platform storage details.

Both entries bootstrap through the projection. Browser shell commands call projection mutations for locale/theme and canvas settings; reactive theme application is shared or installed by platform bootstrap, not coupled to persistence callbacks.

## Invariants

- Both adapters satisfy one compile-time contract and tests import both variants.
- Projection never imports Tauri IPC or browser app-data directly.
- Browser hydration merges durable defaults before entering typed projection state.
- All settings-backed mutations use projection normalization and persistence modes.

title: Decision: Keep one canvas viewport authority
description:
## Decision
Make the camera/viewport module the sole owner and atomic publisher of viewport state, reference scale, and viewport revision; expose a caller-shaped read model through Canvas Query Surface and delete mirrors.

## Rationale

design:
## Selected Design

Keep CameraController as the sole viewport owner and make each mutation publish an immutable viewport read model plus one monotonically increasing revision atomically. Canvas Query Surface exposes this product; ZoomControls and other app callers consume the runtime/query seam.

Delete SceneSession viewport storage, the callback whose ordering updates it, global `view-state` mirrors, the extra `viewportRevision` alias, and dead `zoomReference` presentation input. Retain renderer/chrome consumers through the canonical camera read model.

## Invariants

- A pan/zoom/resize/reference update has one state transition and one revision increment.
- Query consumers observe a coherent state/revision pair.
- Transient viewport state does not become persisted SceneStore authority.
- UI does not import hidden global viewport mirrors.

title: Decide the Scene Interaction Session ownership boundary
description:
## Decision

Scene interaction is one stateful runtime Session. `createSceneInteractionSession()` constructs the tools and fixed interaction collaborators, installs every canvas/window listener, owns the active tool and the single pointer/Space/drag session, encodes routing and refresh order, and tears the whole interaction graph down. Its runtime-facing interface is limited to tool synchronization, viewport refresh, transient history, and idempotent disposal.

## Rationale

The current `SceneInteractionController`, callback-driven `SceneInteractionFrame`, and forwarding `SceneToolModules` divide one lifecycle across three shallow modules. The Frame owns raw listener installation and small pieces of state, while the Controller still chooses pointer priority, commit/cancel order, tool transitions, refresh order, and teardown. This makes ownership claims hard to enforce and leaves `pointercancel` and window blur unhandled, so lost events can strand an edit transaction, captured pointer state, or the Space-held cursor. Those concerns change together and should be hidden behind one deep session boundary.

## Alternatives Considered

- A reducer/statechart kernel with normalized events, ordered effects, correlation IDs, and imperative resource actors. It gives excellent sequence tests, but the synchronous tool and DOM APIs would require a large event/effect protocol and drag-handle registry. The protocol cost is not justified while routing remains local and explicit.
- An internal lifecycle coordinator while retaining `SceneInteractionController` for event routing. It improves cancellation and teardown ordering, but deliberately leaves listener/state/routing ownership split and the oversized controller intact. It is a migration waypoint rather than the desired boundary.
- Keep the callback Frame and add `pointercancel`/blur handlers. This fixes the immediate defect but preserves the shallow handler/state-mutator interface and duplicated lifecycle ownership.
- A generic prioritized participant pipeline. Rejected because the priority among fixed handles, shared gestures, and the active tool is product behavior that should remain explicit and reviewable.
design:
## Interface Contract

`createSceneInteractionSession(deps)` returns a `SceneInteractionSession` with:

```ts
interface SceneInteractionSession {
  setTool(name: string): void
  refreshMeasurements(): void
  canUndoTransientHistory(): boolean
  canRedoTransientHistory(): boolean
  undoTransientHistory(): boolean
  redoTransientHistory(): boolean
  dispose(): void
}
```

Construction attaches listeners and activates the authoritative initial tool. Callers cannot attach/detach listeners, inspect or mutate pointer state, inject raw DOM handlers, or choose cleanup ordering.

## Owned Invariants

- Exactly one Session owns container/window listeners, active-tool identity, Space state, pointer capture identity, generic tool drag state, pending host-focus animation, and all fixed interaction collaborators.
- Pointer-down priority remains explicit: editor/UI exclusions, rotation handle, Zone control point, Measurement Guide control point, pan, active tool, then Select shared gesture.
- Captured pointer movement and release accept only the matching pointer ID. Release commits a generic drag once, completes a shared gesture once, then clears transient state and refreshes in canonical order.
- `pointercancel` and window blur never commit. They abort active direct manipulation and Scene Edit transactions, clear captured/generic drag state, cancel only the active tool's transient capture while preserving a valid passive Polygon draft, clear hover, release Space, restore the active-tool cursor, and refresh presentation.
- A tool transition is a cancellation boundary: abort shared/direct manipulation, cancel inline editing when changing tools, deactivate the previous adapter, activate the new adapter, update cursor, then refresh selection presentation.
- Refresh order is owned in one place and preserves tool drafts during ordinary viewport updates.
- Disposal detaches listeners first, cancels pending focus, aborts transient work, disposes tools and overlays, removes shared DOM, clears hover, and is idempotent. Best-effort cleanup attempts every owned resource before surfacing errors.
- Failed construction must not leave installed listeners or created resources behind.

## Internal Tool Boundary

Keep `SceneToolAdapter` as the varying tool interface. Replace the public method-for-method `SceneToolModules` façade with a private registry that owns adapter lookup, unique iteration, transition, and disposal. The Session routes directly to the active adapter and keeps fixed interaction priority in named code; no generic participant framework is introduced.

## Migration And Testing

Characterize current priority, pointer-up, tool-transition, refresh, focus, and teardown behavior through user-equivalent DOM events. Add failing regressions for pointer cancellation and window blur before production changes. Move listener ownership and interaction state into the Session, then move routing/ordering and internalize the tool registry. Migrate runtime and broad integration tests to the Session seam, delete the superseded Frame handler/state API and controller ownership, and update source-boundary guards plus `docs/agent/canvas-runtime.md`.

Focused tests must cover pointer-ID isolation, cancellation versus commit, Space release, passive Polygon-draft preservation, active direct-manipulation rollback, delayed-focus cancellation, exact listener teardown, tool transitions, transient history, and idempotent disposal. Retain focused adapter tests and the broad Scene runtime integration suite.

## Dependency Strategy

The Session is an internal canvas-runtime module. It reuses existing Scene, camera, tool adapters, transaction coordinator, overlays, and DOM APIs; it adds no runtime dependency and does not alter persisted or IPC contracts.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] One stateful Scene Interaction Session and its small runtime-facing interface are explicit.
- [ ] Listener, pointer, tool-transition, cancellation, refresh, focus-animation, and teardown ownership are recorded.
- [ ] `pointercancel` and window-blur rollback semantics, pointer-ID isolation, Space release, and passive-draft preservation are explicit.
- [ ] The adapter registry remains private and fixed interaction priority remains explicit.
- [ ] Reducer/statechart, lifecycle coordinator, local handler fix, and generic participant alternatives are recorded with rejection reasons.
- [ ] Characterization-first TDD, migration, boundary-test, and subsystem-doc expectations are explicit.
- [ ] Implementation work is represented by a separate bead.
close_reason: Accepted one stateful Scene Interaction Session as the listener, pointer, routing, cancellation, refresh, and teardown owner; retained explicit priority and existing tool adapters without a reducer protocol.

title: Decide shared Scene Arrangement Placement seam
description:
## Decision

Scene arrangement placement is one transaction-owning canvas-runtime operation. Clipboard Paste/Duplicate, Object Stamp, and Saved Object Stamp convert their source into a normalized `SceneArrangementTemplate`, then call `place({ template, translateBy, historyType })`. The operation returns a receipt containing whether placement committed and the cloned top-level selection.

## Rationale

The three production paths independently allocate identities, resolve Zone-name collisions, translate ellipse geometry, remap typed Object Group members, append arrays, and derive selection. Their semantics have already drifted: clipboard paste returns as soon as any cloned Group exists, so a mixed Group-plus-ungrouped arrangement clones every object but omits the ungrouped clone from selection. These are Scene mutation invariants, not tool-specific presentation behavior. One operation makes them reviewable and testable once while guaranteeing that a placement is exactly one undoable Scene Edit.

## Alternatives Considered

- A pure draft-level copier returning selection. It is small and testable, but every caller still assembles transaction, mutation, and selection commit ordering.
- An intent-driven placement command with `clipboard-paste`, `duplicate-selection`, `object-stamp`, and `saved-object-stamp` modes plus Layer refusals. It centralizes too much source policy and creates a mode switch that must grow for unrelated future tools.
- A compile-plan/apply interface. It makes clone plans easy to inspect but exposes a stale interval between destination collision analysis and application, and introduces public plan types that current previews do not need.
- Keep three implementations and fix clipboard selection locally. Rejected because identity, collision, geometry, Group, and selection invariants would continue to drift independently.
design:
## Interface Contract

`SceneArrangementTemplate` is an internal canvas-runtime value, distinct from persisted `.canopi`, clipboard storage, and Saved Object Stamp wire payloads. Each Plant, Zone, Annotation, and Measurement Guide prototype carries an explicit `sourceId` plus its normalized Scene entity. Each Object Group prototype carries its source identity and typed members referring to those source identities. This allows Saved Stamp Zone payload IDs to differ from their user-visible destination names without casts or special cases.

`createSceneArrangementPlacement({ sceneEdits, createId? })` returns one operation:

```ts
place({
  template,
  translateBy,
  historyType,
}): SceneArrangementPlacementReceipt
```

The receipt exposes `committed`, `createdCount`, and `selectedTopLevelIds`. Callers use `committed` for repeated-paste counters and post-placement tool behavior; they do not inspect draft mutation side effects.

## Owned Invariants

- Allocate fresh Plant, Annotation, Measurement Guide, and Object Group identities.
- Allocate collision-safe Zone names against both destination and earlier clones in the same placement.
- Translate ordinary points while translating only the center of ellipse Zone geometry, never its radius vector.
- Reset creation-time lock state and preserve the normalized non-identity prototype fields supplied by the adapter.
- Remap typed Object Group members through one source-to-clone identity map.
- Drop Object Groups with fewer than two successfully remapped members.
- Select every valid cloned Group plus every cloned entity not owned by a valid cloned Group, including mixed Group-plus-ungrouped arrangements and members released by an invalid Group.
- Build clones before appending arrays, then apply entities and selection through exactly one `SceneEditCoordinator.run(historyType, ...)` call.
- Leave the source template immutable and reusable for repeated placement.
- Propagate unexpected allocation or transaction errors so `SceneEditCoordinator` aborts atomically.

## Policy Kept Outside

- Clipboard capture, normal/context-paste offsets, and Paste versus Duplicate pinned-name policy.
- Object Stamp hit sampling, source lock/Layer revalidation, snapping, preview, and repeated placement lifecycle.
- Saved Object Stamp decoding, stripped/unlocked prototype projection, destination Layer checks, snapping, ghost preview, and one-shot tool lifecycle.
- Platform persistence and DOM behavior.

## Migration And Testing

Add interface tests first for mixed Group plus ungrouped Plant selection, typed remapping (including Saved Stamp Zone source ID versus name), multiple Zone collisions, ellipse translation, invalid Group fallback, immutable/reusable templates, empty input, one history edit, and thrown-error rollback. Route Clipboard Paste/Paste At/Duplicate first, then Object Stamp, then Saved Object Stamp. Delete the three clone/remap/name/translation implementations after their callers delegate. Retain caller tests for capture, eligibility, snapping, preview, history label, undo, and tool lifecycle. Add a source-boundary test preventing those placement invariants from returning to caller modules.

## Dependency Strategy

The operation is in-process and internal to `canvas/runtime`. It depends only on Scene entity types, `SceneEditCoordinator`, and the existing UUID helper (replaceable for deterministic tests). It adds no runtime dependency, platform adapter, or cross-app import.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The canonical template and transaction-owning placement receipt are explicit.
- [ ] Identity, Zone collision, ellipse translation, Group remapping, invalid-Group, atomicity, and top-level selection invariants are recorded.
- [ ] Clipboard, Object Stamp, and Saved Object Stamp policies retained outside the module are explicit.
- [ ] Pure copier, intent-mode command, compile-plan/apply, and local-fix alternatives are recorded with rejection reasons.
- [ ] The migration and interface-level TDD strategy are explicit.
- [ ] Implementation work is represented by a separate bead.
close_reason: Accepted a transaction-owning Scene Arrangement Placement seam with normalized source-identity templates and source-specific tool policy retained in adapters.

title: Decide shared Design Session replacement seam
description:
## Decision

Design replacement is an explicit operation behind one platform-neutral Design Session replacement module. The module exposes two operations: attach a Canvas Runtime document surface to the active Design Session, and replace the active Design with a resolved incoming Design. Desktop and Web intent facades keep acquiring files, applying dirty guards, and choosing persistence targets; they delegate the authority handoff to this module. Reactive changes to the non-canvas Design snapshot never trigger canvas hydration.

## Rationale

The Web Edition currently spreads replacement ordering across its Design Session controller and a canvas workspace observer. Canvas scene state is authoritative in SceneStore and is not mirrored into the non-canvas Design snapshot, so observing every snapshot identity can rehydrate stale canvas-owned data after a rename or other Design Edit. Desktop already concentrates the corresponding authority handoff, baseline reset, canvas lifecycle, and workflow ordering. A two-operation in-process module gives both platforms the same invariant without making their genuinely different Browser Draft, native file, confirmation, queue, or autosave policies part of a generic public interface.

## Alternatives Considered

- A generic intent actor with queued jobs, generic source/checkpoint types, and cancellation. It offers future concurrency flexibility but adds speculative interface concepts beyond the current replacement hazard.
- A complete cross-platform Design Session facade owning New, Open, Template, Draft, Save, autosave, runtime mounting, and persistence adapters. It gives callers simple product verbs but requires several new seams and a broad migration before the authority bug can be removed.
- Keep separate desktop and Web replacement paths and add a narrower observer guard. Rejected because callers would still need to infer replacement from mutable snapshot identity and maintain duplicate ordering.
design:
## Interface Contract

The Design Session replacement module has two caller-facing operations:

- `attach(canvas)` reads the active Design once. If a Design exists, it performs initial canvas hydration; otherwise it presents the empty attached state.
- `replace(input, canvas)` accepts a resolved incoming Design, its semantic normalization kind (`new` or `loaded`), saved-path identity, display name, and an optional attached canvas. It returns an applied receipt including whether canvas hydration occurred.

Both operations are synchronous after the caller has acquired and validated the incoming source. Source acquisition, dirty confirmation, cancellation, queue management, and persistence remain in the platform intent facades.

## Invariants And Ordering

- SceneStore is the sole canvas authority while a canvas is attached.
- Canvas hydration occurs only through `attach` or `replace`; Design Edit and other non-canvas snapshot changes never invoke either operation implicitly.
- Normalization completes before mutation.
- Initial attachment loads the current Design without replacing canonical Design Session state or resetting baselines.
- Explicit attached replacement replaces the canvas Design, updates Design Session identity, resets dirty baselines, clears history, shows canvas chrome, zooms to fit, and installs Design Session workflows.
- Explicit detached replacement updates Design Session identity, resets dirty baselines, and installs workflows without canvas calls.
- Empty attachment hides canvas chrome and installs the appropriate Design Session workflow scope.
- Operational failures propagate to the platform facade; the replacement module does not translate I/O or picker cancellation.

## Hidden Complexity

The implementation owns new-versus-loaded normalization, initial-load-versus-replacement choice, attached/detached authority handoff, store identity updates, dirty-baseline ordering, canvas history/chrome/zoom ordering, and workflow installation. Callers do not assemble those steps.

## Dependency Strategy

The module is in-process. It is composed with a Design Session store and workflow runner, and it accepts the existing Canvas Runtime document surface when attached. No new external adapter is introduced. The two real platform adapters remain at the existing compile-time edges: native file/dialog/persistence behavior for desktop and browser file/Browser Draft behavior for Web.

## Consequences And Migration

- The Web Design Session controller keeps its current caller-facing commands but delegates resolved replacements and attachment.
- The Web canvas workspace stops observing the Design snapshot and deletes its local load/replace helper.
- The desktop Design Session state machine delegates its existing apply and attach ordering to the same module while retaining dirty guards, queued loads, state reporting, autosave, and teardown.
- Shared replacement code must import neither Tauri nor browser infrastructure. Web bundle native-import guards remain in force.
- This restores the accepted consequences of the Web Design format, Browser Draft, and compile-time adapter decisions; no ADR is reopened.

## Testing Strategy

- Add interface-level replacement tests for empty attach, initial attach, attached replacement, detached replacement, new/loaded normalization, and workflow ordering.
- Add a Web regression proving a non-canvas Design Edit does not call canvas replacement or erase live SceneStore-owned data.
- Preserve desktop transition tests for dirty guard, cancellation, queued load, state reporting, autosave, and teardown; migrate duplicated post-load assertions only after the shared interface covers them.
- Replace the Web source guard that forbids all shared Design Session modules with a precise guard allowing the platform-neutral replacement module while continuing to reject Tauri, IPC, and desktop lifecycle imports.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The selected attach/replace interface and Design Session seam are explicit.
- [ ] Canvas authority, normalization, ordering, and error invariants are recorded.
- [ ] Platform-specific acquisition, dirty guard, queue, and persistence policies remain outside the module.
- [ ] The actor, full facade, and observer-guard alternatives are recorded with rejection reasons.
- [ ] ADR compatibility and the test migration strategy are explicit.
- [ ] Implementation work is represented by a separate bead.
close_reason: Accepted shared attach/replace Design Session seam with platform-specific acquisition and persistence retained at compile-time edges.

title: Collapse mobile Species Catalog filters
description:
## Slice Summary
Make the Web Edition Species Catalog Workbench bottom sheet show the Species list immediately on mobile and small-screen layouts by collapsing supported filter controls into a one-line summary by default.

## User Value
Mobile users can browse Species rows without Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle controls consuming the constrained bottom-sheet height, while still being able to expand and use those filters when needed.

## Out of Scope
Do not add new Species Catalog Filters, expand Web Edition catalog data scope, change desktop Species Catalog behavior, or redesign every Web Edition side panel.
design:
## Agent Brief
**Category:** feature
**Summary:** Collapse Web Edition Species Catalog Filter controls by default in mobile bottom-sheet layouts.

**Current behavior:**
On mobile and smaller tablet Web Edition layouts, the Species Catalog Workbench renders as a bottom sheet. The supported Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle filter controls are always expanded above the Species list, which can leave too little visible space for browsing rows.

**Desired behavior:**
In mobile and small-screen layouts, the Species Catalog Workbench shows a compact one-line filter summary by default. The summary communicates that Species Catalog Filters are available, exposes active-filter state, and lets the user expand or collapse the full supported filter controls. When expanded, the current Workbench-backed Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle controls keep the same behavior as today, including active chips and Clear All. Desktop-width behavior should not be regressed.

**Key interfaces:**
- Web Edition Species Catalog Workbench filter strip projection
- Generated Web-supported Species Catalog Filter projection
- Active Species Catalog Filter chip behavior
- Browser App Shell small-screen bottom-sheet layout
- i18n strings for filter summary and expand/collapse controls

**Out of scope:**
- Adding new Species Catalog Filters or Web catalog data
- Changing desktop Species Catalog Workbench behavior
- Changing Species Catalog Search ordering or adapter performance
- Touch-safe Plant Stamp placement, which is tracked separately
- A general responsive panel framework for every Web Edition side panel
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Mobile and small-screen Web Edition layouts render the Species Catalog Filter area collapsed into a one-line summary by default.
- [ ] The collapsed summary exposes active-filter state, including a count or equivalent concise indication when filters are active.
- [ ] The summary has accessible expand/collapse behavior and does not overflow its row at phone-width layouts.
- [ ] Expanding the summary reveals the current Web-supported Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle controls only when backed by the Workbench-supported filter projection.
- [ ] Expanded filter controls preserve current toggle, active chip removal, and Clear All behavior.
- [ ] Unsupported desktop-only Species Catalog Filters remain hidden in Web Edition.
- [ ] The Species list remains visible and scrollable in the mobile bottom sheet with filters collapsed.
- [ ] New user-visible strings are added to all supported UI locales.
- [ ] Focused Web Species Catalog panel tests cover collapsed summary, expanded controls, active state, chip removal, Clear All, and unsupported-filter absence.
- [ ] TypeScript check passes.
close_reason: Implemented compact Web Edition Species Catalog filter summary for mobile layouts, preserving desktop filter behavior and Workbench-backed active chip/clear behavior. Verified with npm test -- --run src/__tests__/web-species-catalog-panel.test.tsx, npm test -- --run src/__tests__/i18n-completeness.test.ts, and npx tsc --noEmit.

title: Verify mobile and tablet Species placement UX
description:

## Out of Scope

- [ ] Opening the Web Edition Species Catalog Workbench shows the Species list with filters collapsed by default.
- [ ] Expanding and collapsing the filter summary works with touch input.

close_reason: Verified mobile and tablet Web Edition Species placement UX. title: PRD: Mobile Web Edition Species Catalog placement UX
description:
## Problem Statement

On mobile and smaller tablet screens, the Web Edition Species Catalog Workbench opens as a bottom sheet. The supported filter controls for Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle consume too much of that constrained height, so users cannot immediately see enough Species rows to choose plants comfortably.

The same workflow also depends on native HTML drag/drop from Species rows to the canvas. That is acceptable as an additional desktop and pointer-device path, but it is not reliable enough to be the primary touchscreen workflow. A mobile user needs to browse Species, understand active Species Catalog Filters, and place Placed Plants into the Design with ordinary touch gestures.

## Solution

Improve the mobile Web Edition Species Catalog Workbench so the Species list remains the primary surface in the bottom sheet and plant placement works reliably on touchscreens.

On mobile and small-screen layouts, collapse the supported Species Catalog Filter controls into a one-line summary by default. The summary should show that filters are available, expose active-filter state, and provide an expand/collapse control. When expanded, the user can use the same Web-supported Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle controls and active filter actions already backed by the Species Catalog Workbench.

Add a touch-friendly placement path for Species rows: a visible Place action starts Plant Stamp from that Species, then the user taps the canvas to place the Placed Plant. Native drag/drop remains available where the browser and pointer device support it, but touch users are not forced through drag/drop.

## Success Criteria

- On mobile-width Web Edition layouts, opening the Species Catalog Workbench shows the Species list with supported filters collapsed into a one-line summary by default.
- The collapsed filter summary communicates active-filter state and can expand to the full Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle controls.
- Expanded filter controls preserve current Web-supported filtering behavior, active chips, and Clear All behavior.
- Touchscreen users can start Plant Stamp from a Species row through a visible Place action, then tap the canvas to create a Placed Plant.
- Existing pointer-device drag/drop from Species rows still works.
- Catalog row selection, Species detail, favorite toggling, search, load more, and reduced Web Species Detail behavior are not regressed.
- The implementation uses the existing Species Catalog Workbench, generated Web-supported filter projection, Plant Stamp source seam, and canvas command surfaces.
- Focused Web Species Catalog tests, Plant Stamp seam coverage, responsive mobile/tablet smoke coverage, and TypeScript checks pass.

## User Stories

1. As a mobile Web Edition user, I want the Species Catalog Workbench bottom sheet to show Species rows immediately, so that I can browse plants without the filter area hiding the list.
2. As a mobile Web Edition user, I want a one-line filter summary with expand/collapse behavior, so that I can access filters only when I need them and return quickly to the Species list.
3. As a mobile Web Edition user, I want the collapsed filter summary to show when filters are active, so that I understand why the visible Species list changed.
4. As a mobile Web Edition user, I want to apply, remove, and clear Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle filters from the expanded filter area, so that mobile filtering remains equivalent to the current Web-supported Species Catalog Filter behavior.
5. As a touchscreen user, I want a Place action on a Species row, so that I can start Plant Stamp placement without relying on browser drag/drop.
6. As a touchscreen user, I want to tap the canvas after choosing Place, so that I can create a Placed Plant reliably with normal touch input.
7. As a tablet or desktop pointer-device user, I want existing Species row drag/drop to keep working, so that the current fast placement workflow is not regressed.
8. As a maintainer, I want mobile placement to use the existing Plant Stamp source and canvas command surfaces, so that Web Edition UI does not duplicate Plant Stamp state or bypass Scene Edit ownership.

## Implementation Decisions

- The work is scoped to the Web Edition Species Catalog Workbench and the Browser App Shell's existing small-screen layout. It does not change desktop Species Catalog behavior.
- The supported Web Edition Species Catalog Filter scope remains unchanged: Climate Zone, Habit, and Life Cycle where backed by the generated Web-supported filter projection.
- Unsupported desktop-only Species Catalog Filters remain hidden in Web Edition. This PRD does not add new catalog data, new Parquet shards, new filter metadata, or new Species Detail fields.
- Mobile and small-screen Web Edition layouts should collapse the full filter controls by default into a one-line filter summary. Expanded filters should reuse the current Workbench-backed filter controls rather than hardcoding a separate mobile-only filter model.
- The collapsed filter summary should expose active-filter state using Workbench projections such as active filter count and active chips. It should be accessible as an expand/collapse control and must avoid multi-line overflow in translated UI.
- Expanded filter controls should preserve current behavior for toggling choices, active chips, and Clear All.
- The touch placement path should add a row-level Place action for Species rows in catalog, favorites, and recently viewed lists where Species placement is supported.
- The Place action should start Plant Stamp from the selected Species through the existing Plant Stamp source seam and canvas command surface. It should not assemble drag payloads by hand, mutate canvas scene data directly, or add a second placement state.
- Existing native drag/drop payload behavior should remain available for pointer devices and browsers that support it.
- Row selection/detail behavior, favorite toggling, load-more behavior, search, and existing filter behavior should remain intact. The Place action must not accidentally trigger row detail selection or favorite toggling.
- New user-visible strings for filter summary state, expand/collapse controls, and Place actions must go through i18n and be added to all supported UI locales.
- The first implementation should prefer focused mobile bottom-sheet and touch-placement improvements over a broader side-panel redesign. A larger responsive panel system can be considered later if this focused change is insufficient.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should verify observable user behavior through the Web Edition Species Catalog Workbench and Plant Stamp source seam, not private component state.
- Web Species Catalog panel tests should cover the collapsed mobile filter summary, expand/collapse behavior, active filter count or active state presentation, active chip removal, and Clear All behavior.
- Web Species Catalog panel tests should verify that unsupported filters remain absent and that expanded controls still come from the Workbench-supported filter projection.
- Web Species Catalog panel tests should cover the Place action from catalog rows, favorites, and recently viewed Species. The test should prove that Place starts Plant Stamp through the existing source/command seam and does not rely on native drag/drop.
- Existing Plant Stamp source tests already cover beginning Plant Stamp through a command surface; keep or extend that seam-level coverage if the interface changes.
- Existing Scene Interaction tests already cover Plant Stamp tap/click placement, locked Plants Layer blocking, snapping, source cleanup, and drag/drop placement. Reuse those as the proof that the canvas placement side remains correct.
- Responsive or browser-level smoke coverage should include a mobile viewport and a tablet viewport with the Species Catalog Workbench open as a bottom sheet. The smoke should verify that the Species list is visible with filters collapsed and that touch-style placement can be completed.
- Run focused Web Species Catalog tests and TypeScript checks for implementation. Broader frontend tests should run if the change touches shared panel layout, shell navigation, canvas runtime, or Plant Stamp behavior.

## Out of Scope

- Expanding the Web Edition Species Catalog data scope.
- Adding desktop-only filters, More Filters fields without Web backing data, Site Adaptation, compatibility checks, or replacement suggestions.
- Changing the Web Edition Species Catalog search ordering or DuckDB-WASM catalog performance.
- Replacing the Browser App Shell, redesigning every side panel, or adding a general mobile panel framework beyond what this workflow requires.
- Changing desktop Species Catalog Workbench behavior.
- Removing existing pointer-device drag/drop behavior.
- Adding offline/PWA behavior, service workers, backend persistence, accounts, sync, or cloud libraries.
- Changing Web Edition Plant Detail beyond preserving the current reduced detail surface.

## Further Notes

- The main UX risk is adding a Place action but leaving the user without enough visible canvas space or context to complete placement. Implementation should ensure the bottom sheet, collapsed filters, and active Plant Stamp state make the next canvas tap obvious and reachable on phone and tablet screens.
- Native HTML drag/drop should not be used as the acceptance standard for touchscreen placement. The touch-safe Place action plus canvas tap is the reliable path.
- Text length in the collapsed filter summary needs attention across all 11 UI languages; the summary should degrade to concise labels or counts rather than overflowing its row.
- If the focused bottom-sheet fix still leaves too little workspace on very small screens, a later slice can consider a broader responsive side-panel pattern, such as temporary sheet dismissal after Place or a compact placement confirmation strip.
close_reason: Closed after all three child beads shipped and passed verification: mobile/tablet filter summary, touch-safe Place action, and end-to-end phone/tablet UX checks are complete with focused tests and Web Edition build passing.

title: Performance Evidence and NDJSON Retirement
description:
## Slice Summary
Record before and after evidence for Web catalog browse, two-character search, backed filter use, and locale switching, then remove production dependence on the JavaScript full-catalog NDJSON scan path.

## User Value
Maintainers can verify that the Web catalog migration improved the right paths and that production no longer depends on the old eager scan behavior.

## Out of Scope
Benchmarking unrelated app startup work, expanding Species data scope, and changing website hosting are separate work.
design:
## Agent Brief
**Category:** task
**Summary:** Record Web catalog performance evidence and retire production dependence on the eager NDJSON scan path.

**Current behavior:**
The Web catalog can rely on eager JavaScript data loading and full-catalog scans. The Parquet migration needs recorded evidence that the browser query path improves the intended user workflows and that production no longer depends on the old scan behavior.

**Desired behavior:**
Before landing the migration as complete, maintainers can inspect recorded before/after evidence for browse, two-character active search, backed filter use, and locale switching. Production Web catalog code no longer depends on the expanded NDJSON full-catalog scan path, though small fixtures or transitional tests may remain where explicitly useful.

**Key interfaces:**
- Web Species Catalog performance evidence
- Browse and search query paths
- Backed filter query path
- Locale switching behavior
- Production catalog artifact selection

**Out of scope:**
- Benchmarking unrelated app startup work
- Expanding Species data scope
- Website hosting changes
- Removing useful fixtures that are not on the production path
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Before/after timings are recorded for browse, two-character active search, a backed filter, and locale switching.
- [ ] The evidence identifies dataset size, browser or test environment, and the query path being measured.
- [ ] Production Web catalog behavior uses the Parquet/DuckDB path rather than an eager JavaScript full-catalog NDJSON scan.
- [ ] Any remaining NDJSON usage is limited to fixtures, transitional tests, or explicitly non-production tooling.

description:

title: Localized Web Species Search
description:
